title: Measuring skill activation across agents is harder than it looks
body_markdown:
A coding agent gets much better at a domain when you hand it curated instructions instead of making it reason from scratch. We package those instructions as *skills* : self-contained folders that each teach one thing, like authoring a UiPath RPA workflow, building a UiPath Maestro™ flow, or scaffolding an agent. Over time the library grows to dozens of them.


You can’t pour dozens of skills into the context window at once. The standard answer is **progressive disclosure** : the agent keeps only a one-line description of each skill in view and loads a skill’s full instructions only when it decides that skill is relevant.


That puts a lot of weight on one decision. A skill that is excellent but never gets picked up is worth nothing, so *“did the right skill activate?”* is a first-class quality metric for us. We run the same tasks against Claude Code, Codex, and Google’s Antigravity, and we want one activation number that means the same thing on all three.


That turned out to be harder than it looks. There are three places where “ *did the agent use the skill?”* is more slippery than it sounds, and getting any of them wrong invents a gap between agents that isn’t real.


### All three agents load skills the same way


At the start the agent sees only metadata: every skill’s name and one-line description. When it decides a skill is relevant it loads that skill’s SKILL.md, and that load is the moment the skill is *activated* . If it needs more detail it reads a sub-file under the skill, say references/bindings.md, and that counts as activating the same skill too. All three agents work this way.


What the principle doesn’t fix is how “loading a skill” shows up in the recorded trace. That is where the agents diverge.


### Subtlety one: activating a skill has no single shape


Claude Code has a dedicated Skill tool, so activating a skill leaves an explicit event: Skill("maestro-flow"). Codex and Antigravity have no such tool. They activate a skill by opening its files, the same way they would open any other file. We checked this against real runs: an Antigravity trace that uses the Maestro flow skill simply reads skills/uipath-maestro-flow/SKILL.md, and Codex does the same through the shell. There is no “I invoked a skill” event, so activation has to be inferred from the files the agent touched.


That is the trap we fell into first. Our initial detector looked only for the Skill tool call. Claude Code lit up on every task while Codex and Antigravity looked like they never touched a skill, even on tasks they solved correctly. We had built a Claude-shaped detector and called it a cross-agent metric.


The split isn’t even clean by agent. Both shapes show up inside a single Claude Code trace: when a task could involve more than one skill, the agent often calls Skill("planner") for the first and then reads the second skill’s SKILL.md directly, as a plain file read rather than a tool call.


So the fix is to accept either signal from every agent: the tool call, or a skills/<name>/ path in whatever the agent read or ran. Claude needs the file-read half as much as Codex does.


### Subtlety two: activation is not a single moment


Inferring activation from file access brings judgment calls with it. The first is separating looking from loading: listing the skills directory to see what exists activates nothing, so it cannot count. Reading a *different* skill’s files is a real activation, but of that skill, which is what turns one signal into a precision measure as well as a recall one. The second is which skills count when several are activated in one run. Routing makes that the normal case rather than an edge case. Take a request to pull invoices out of a shared mailbox and key them into SAP:


1. The agent reads the skill listing, decides the request needs planning first, and calls Skill("uipath-planner").
2. The planner’s instructions tell it to work out how many projects the request spans, then hand the build to whichever skill owns the artifact.
3. The agent reads skills/uipath-rpa/SKILL.md directly, as a plain file read rather than a tool call, to get the authoring rules.
4. It builds the workflow and validates it.


The task carries a criterion for each skill, and both should pass. Two obvious rules get that wrong. One fails the row as soon as an unexpected skill appears, so uipath-planner at step 1 decides the uipath-rpa criterion before step 3 can happen. The other scores only the first activation, so uipath-planner passes and uipath-rpa reads as never having fired. **We count a skill activated anywhere in the run, in any order.** Activating uipath-planner is a step toward uipath-rpa, not a vote against it.


**The run can also stop early: once the expected skill is activated, the answer cannot change, so there is no reason to keep paying for turns.** On Claude Code we stop it right there, instead of burning a whole turn budget while sitting on an answer from turn one.


### Subtlety three: the description is not the same length across agents


This one surprised us most. The thing whose activation we’re measuring, the one-line description, doesn’t reach every agent intact.


Each agent truncates the skill listing at its own limit before the model sees it, and the limits differ. Claude Code cuts at about 1,500 characters, our skills repository caps each description at 1,024 to stay clear of that, and Codex and Antigravity draw their own lines. Anything past an agent’s limit is invisible on that agent.


The consequence is about ordering. Two ways to describe the same Maestro flow skill:


> ***Buried:*** ** A comprehensive skill offering best practices and detailed guidance for designing, building, and maintaining long-running business processes and orchestrations, including advice on when they are appropriate and, further down, on authoring *.flow* and *.bpmn* files.


> ***Front-loaded:*** ** Author *.flow* and *.bpmn* Maestro orchestrations: triggers, bindings, error handling, long-running process design.


The first hides its most identifying detail, the .flow / .bpmn signal, at the end of a long sentence, exactly the part a tighter agent cuts. On that agent the skill reads like generic “best practices” prose and misfires. The second leads with the identity and the file extensions, so it survives every cutoff and fires consistently. The fix is just putting the identifying signal first.


### An explicit trigger in each description lifted recall 21 points


Only once the detector was fair across all three agents did a change to a skill’s description produce a number worth acting on, rather than an artifact of which harness we happened to run. That is the whole reason the three subtleties matter. The intervention that helped most was simple: add an explicit **“always invoke for X”** line to each skill’s description, tied to a signal unique to that skill (Always invoke for .uipx files, Always invoke for .xaml or .cs workflow files, and so on).


Why it works follows from progressive disclosure. Activation hinges entirely on that short description, since everything else about the skill is invisible until after it’s picked. A vague summary leaves the call to the model’s judgment; an explicit trigger bound to a unique marker gives it a concrete reason to fire. Front-loaded, the anchor stays inside every agent’s cutoff, so nothing about the fix depends on which agent has the most room.


Micro-recall rose from 46.3% to 67.3%, and mean per-skill recall from 0.48 to 0.68. The biggest gains came from skills that had been nearly invisible: diagnostics 0.16 to 0.68, maestro-flow 0.32 to 0.72, agents 0.16 to 0.56, human-in-the-loop 0.33 to 0.70, rpa-legacy 0.41 to 0.77. The skills also didn’t start firing when they shouldn’t: precision held around 0.96 and the out-of-scope prompts stayed correctly declined.


### In Coder Eval, the whole check is one criterion


Running this is low-effort in[Coder Eval](https://coder-eval.com/) . All three subtleties sit behind one declarative criterion: you state which skill should fire, and the framework works out what “fired” means for the agent under test. The routed invoice task becomes this:


```text
task_id: skill-planner-invoice-routing  tags: [uipath-planner, integration, mode:build]   initial_prompt: |    Pull invoices out of the shared mailbox and key them into SAP. Load    whichever UiPath skills you need, then build the automation and    validate it.   success_criteria:    - type: skill_triggered      description: "Agent activated the uipath-planner skill"      skill_name: uipath-planner      expected_skill: uipath-planner      weight: 2.0
```


That is the entire declaration. Add one per skill and each gets its own verdict, so neither can spoil the other, and stacked across the suite they turn activation into a classification problem with precision and recall. No evaluation framework we know of treats skill activation as a first-class criterion.


### Conclusion


A detector keyed to Claude’s Skill call reads Codex and Antigravity as never using skills, on tasks they solve correctly. Activation is not a single moment either, so a run that routes through one skill on its way to another reads as a failure unless you decide otherwise on purpose. The description being matched reaches each agent cut to a different length, so the same skill fires on one and misfires on another depending on where the cut lands. Handle all three the same way everywhere and an intervention becomes readable: front-loading an explicit trigger into each description moved micro-recall from 46.3% to 67.3%, with precision steady near 0.96. Get one of the three wrong and the chart measures the checker instead of the skills.


### References


- Anthropic, **“Agent Skills”** (Claude Code documentation) — progressive disclosure; the instruction to put the key use case first in a skill’s description, and to make the description more specific when a skill fails to activate; and the 1,536-character truncation of description plus when_to_use in the skill listing.[https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md)
- **Agent Skills** — the open standard the SKILL.md format follows, and the reason all three agents implement progressive disclosure the same way.[https://agentskills.io](https://agentskills.io/)
- **Coder Eval** — the open-source harness the activation suite runs on.[https://github.com/UiPath/coder_eval](https://github.com/UiPath/coder_eval)
- **Coder Eval, the** skill_triggered **criterion** — the agent-agnostic detector described here: the Skill tool call, the skills/<name>/ path match, and the any-activation scoring rule.[https://coder-eval.com/docs/task-definition-guide#skill_triggered](https://coder-eval.com/docs/task-definition-guide#skill_triggered)
